# Royalties paid to non-resident - two-tier discount (pwc)
1. With the introduction of two-tier profits tax rates, there are two possible sets of domestic WHT rates on royalties paid to non-resident corporations:
	- i.	If the two-tier tax rates apply, the WHT rates are 2.475% for the first HKD 6.67 million of gross royalty income (i.e. the deemed profit rate of 30% times the tax rate of 8.25% for the first HKD 2 million of assessable profits) and 4.95% for the remaining amount of gross royalty income (i.e. the deemed profit rate of 30% times the tax rate of 16.5% for the remaining amount of assessable profits).
	- ii	If the two two-tier tax rates do not apply, the WHT rate for the whole amount of gross royalty income is 4.95%.  
	- iii	The 2.475% and 4.95% rates are determined by applying the relevant two-tier rates, which are 8.25% and 16.5%, respectively, on the deemed assessable profits of the royalties. In the normal situation, the deemed assessable profits are 30% of the royalties received by or accrued to a non-resident corporation. Hence, the effective WHT rate on the royalties ranges from 2.475% (when the deemed assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 4.95% (in relation to the deemed assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two-tier rates are not applicable).

	- In the situation where a person carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong has, at any time, wholly or partly owned the IP in respect of which the royalties are paid and the non-resident corporation is an associate of the Hong Kong payer, the deemed assessable profits are 100% of the royalties received by or accrued to a non-resident corporation. Hence, the applicable WHT rates are 8.25% for the first HKD 2 million of assessable profits and 16.5% for the remaining amount if the two-tier rates are applicable.
2. The domestic WHT rate on the gross royalty income ranges from 2.475% (when the assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 4.95% (in relation to the assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two tier-rates are not applicable), capped at 3% according to the treaty.
3. For payments for the use of, or the right to use, aircraft, the effective WHT rate ranges from 2.475% on the gross payments (when the assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 3% (in relation to the assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two tier-rates are not applicable). For other cases, the effective WHT rate on the gross royalty income ranges from 2.475% (when the assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 4.95% (in relation to the assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two tier-rates are not applicable).
	4	Since a rate specified in the treaty is higher than the domestic WHT rates, the effective WHT rate on the gross royalty income ranges from 2.475% (when the assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 4.95% (in relation to the assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two tier-rates are not applicable).
	5	The domestic WHT rate on the gross royalty income ranges from 2.475% (when the assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 4.95% (in relation to the assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two tier-rates are not applicable), capped at 4% according to the treaty.
	6	The 0% rate applies to payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment or for information concerning industrial, commercial, or scientific experience. For other cases, the WHT rate on the gross royalty income ranges from 2.475% (when the assessable profits are HKD 2 million or less and the two-tier rates are applicable) to 4.95% (in relation to the assessable profits in excess of HKD 2 million when the two-tier rates are applicable or when the two tier-rates are not applicable), capped at 3% according to the treaty.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/chargeable

# Taxation of corporate treasury centres
A corporate treasury centre ('CTC') is an in-house bank within a group. A typical CTC performs the functions of:
(a) Intra-group financing;
(b) Multi-currency cash management and liquidity management;
(c) Cash pooling;
(d) Central or regional processing of payments to vendors or suppliers;
(e) Conducting transactions for financial or treasury-related risk management; and
(f) Supporting the raising of capital by the group.

To attract multinational and Mainland enterprises to establish global or regional CTCs in Hong Kong, the Inland Revenue (Amendment) (No. 2) Ordinance 2016 was enacted on 3 June 2016 to:
(a) Provide a [[s.14D Concessionary profits tax rate for qualifying corporate treasury centres (QCTCs)]];
(b) Introduce new [[s.16(2)(g) deduction rules for interest expenses incurred by intra-group financing businesses]];  and
(c) Introduce new [[s.15(1)(ia) deeming provisions for interest income and other gains from intra-group financing businesses]].

The IRD issued DIPN 52 in September 2016 to provide guidance on the application of the profits tax provisions in relation to CTCs.

[[CTC example (2)]]
# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# s.14D Concessionary profits tax rate for qualifying corporate treasury centres (QCTCs)
[[Qualifying corporate treasury centres (QCTCs)]] can enjoy 50% reduction of the profits tax rate, i.e. 8.25% for the **qualifying income** from [[corporate treasury activities]], which accrued on or after 1 April 2016.

[[Qualifying profits at concessionary tax rate of 8.25%]]

[[CTC example]]
---- 
## Election for the concessionary tax rate
An election in writing to apply the **concessionary tax rate** must be made, which is ~irrevocable~ as long as the CTC remains as a QCTC (ss.14D(5)(b) and (6)).

If a CTC which previously qualified as a QCTC **fails to qualify** as a QCTC in a given year of assessment, it will not qualify for the concessionary tax rate for that year of assessment and the subsequent year of assessment despite that it may meet the conditions of a QCTC in the subsequent year of assessment (s.14D(7)). Once disqualified, the election ceases to be effective and the CTC needs to make a fresh election when it qualifies as a QCTC again.

If a QCTC incurs a **tax loss** from corporate treasury operations, it would not be disqualified but the tax loss can only be set off against its other types of profits taxed at half rate; or against other profits taxed at normal rates after making the adjustment as required under ss.19CA and 19CB (discussed in section 13.6 on 'Unabsorbed loss from normal and concessionary trading receipts').
# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# Qualifying corporate treasury centres (QCTCs)
A CTC qualifies as a 'qualifying corporate treasury centre' ('QCTC') if (ss.14D(2) and (3)):

(a) It is a [[standalone entity]] carrying out one or more of the following [[corporate treasury activities]] in Hong Kong:
	* (i) Carrying on an [[intra-group financing business]];
	* (ii) Providing [[corporate treasury services]] to a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]];
	* (iii) Entering into [[corporate treasury transaction]]s with a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]]; or
(b) It satisfies the specified [[safe harbour rule under s.14E]], i.e. not lower than 75% of its profits and assets are corporate treasury profits and assets; or
(c) It has obtained the CIR's determination that it is a QCTC under s.14F(1).

The CTC must also meet the **business substance requirements** in s.14D(5):
(a) The central management and control of the CTC must be exercised in Hong Kong (the central management and control requirement).
(b) The activities that produce the qualifying profits must be either
	* (i) Carried out in Hong Kong by the CTC; or
	* (ii) Arranged by the CTC to be carried out in Hong Kong (the substantial activity requirement).

S.14D(9) specifies that a FI is not eligible to be a QCTC.

---- 
# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# corporate treasury activities
'Corporate treasury activity' is defined in s.14C(1) as

(a) The carrying on an [[intra-group financing business]] (the business of the borrowing of money from and lending of money to an associated corporation);
(b) Providing a [[corporate treasury service]] to an associated corporation; or
(c) Entering into a [[corporate treasury transaction]] undertaken on its own account and related to the business of an associated corporation.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# intra-group financing business
'Intra-group financing business' is defined in s.14C(1) to mean, in relation to a corporation, the business of the borrowing of money from and lending of money to its associated corporations.
---- 
## Carrying on an intra-group financing business
In a typical intra-group financing arrangement, group entities remit excess cash into a centralised pool, which is managed by a designated entity, a CTC. A corporation will only be regarded as acting in the ordinary course of its intra-group financing business where it borrows money from and lends money to its associated corporations regularly as a business with a view to earning an interest margin (DIPN 52, para 9). There must be a sufficient number of intra-group borrowing and lending transactions with a number of associated corporations, involving not an insignificant amount of funds having regard to the nature and scale of the business operations of the group concerned. The IRD will generally accept that a corporation is carrying on an intra-group financing business if (DIPN 52, para 10):
(a) It has **not less than ~four~ borrowing or lending transactions each month**;
(b) ~Each~ borrowing or lending transaction **exceeds $250,000**; and
(c) Borrowing or lending transactions are with **not less than four associated corporations** in the relevant basis period.

Failure to reach the above presumptive benchmark would ~not necessarily lead to~ the conclusion that the corporation is not carrying on an intra-group financing business. The IRD will make an ~assessment based on facts~, taking into account the following factors (DIPN 52, para 9):
(a) The frequency, repetitiveness and the amount of the borrowing from and lending to associated corporations of money;
(b) Whether there is borrowing from and lending to associated corporations of money at commercial rates of interest;
(c) Whether there is a degree of system and continuity of laying out and getting back of the loan of money by way of interest and repayment of principal;
(d) The regularity and frequency of payment of interest and repayment of principal;
(e) Whether a profit is earned out of the interest differential between the borrowing and lending; and
(f) Whether the interest charged on the borrowing and lending is on an arm's length basis.

The IRD reiterated in DIPN 52 that the arm's length principle must be followed when fixing the interest rates for intra-group financing transactions, and transfer pricing adjustments may be made by the IRD.

However, a corporation that only borrows and lends money in isolated transactions would not be regarded as carrying on an intra-group financing business. On the other hand, a corporation may carry on other businesses in addition to the intra-group financing business; and a corporation may qualify even though it is largely funded by equity or bank loans.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# corporate treasury service
'Corporate treasury service' is defined in s.1 of Schedule 17B to mean any of the following services provided to an associated corporation:
(a) Managing the cash and liquidity position;
(b) Processing payments to the vendors or suppliers;
(c) Managing relationships with FIs;
(d) Providing corporate finance advisory services;
(e) Advising on the management of the investment of the funds;
(f) Managing investor relations;
(g) Providing guarantees, performance bonds, standby letters of credit or other credit risk instruments, or services in relation to remittances;
(h) Providing advice or service in relation to the management of interest rate risk, foreign exchange risk, liquidity risk, credit risk, commoditiy risk or other financial risk;
(i) Providing assistance in merger or acquisition;
(j) Providing advice or service in relation to compliance with accounting standards, internal treasury policies or regulatory requirements;
(k) Providing advice or service in relation to operations of the treasury management system; and
(l) Providing business planning and co-ordination in connection with any of the above activities.
---- 
Cash forecasting and cash pooling (including physical cash pooling and notional cash pooling) are within the scope of corporate treasury service, but re-invoicing transactions are neither corporate treasury services nor corporate treasury transactions, and the half rate concession will not apply (DIPN 52, para 63 and 67).

Where a QCTC enters into a corporate treasury service contract with a non-Hong Kong associated corporation which in turn enters into a back-to-back service contract on the same terms with a Hong Kong associated corporation, the IRD takes the view that the corporate treasury service is, in substance, provided by the QCTC to the Hong Kong associated corporation. Such service is not considered as a qualifying corporate treasury service and the half rate concession will not apply (DIPN 52, para 83).

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# corporate treasury transaction
'Corporate treasury transaction' is defined in s.2 of Schedule 17B to mean any of the following transactions that is entered into by a corporation on its own account and related to the business of an [[associated corporation]]:
(a) Providing guarantees, performance bonds, standby letters of credit or other credit risk instruments;
(b) Investing the funds of the corporation or associated corporation in deposits, certificates of deposit, bonds, notes, debentures, money-market funds or other financial instruments for managing the cash and liquidity position;
(c) Entering into contracts (e.g. contracts for difference, foreign exchange contracts, forward/futures contracts, swap contracts, options contracts) for hedging interest rate risk, foreign exchange risk, liquidity risk, credit risk, commodity risk or other financial risk; and
(d) Factoring or forfaiting transactions.
---- 
Corporate treasury transactions may be concluded with Hong Kong entities (e.g. placing a deposit with a Hong Kong bank) as long as they are related to the business of a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]].

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# non-Hong Kong associated corporation
'Non-Hong Kong associated corporation' means an associated corporation that does not carry on any trade, profession or business in Hong Kong (s.14C(1) ).

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# CTC example
Example 27 (Adapted from DIPN 52, Example 20)

CTC-HK is a QCTC within a multinational group of companies. It provided to its associated corporations the following services:
(a) providing advice in relation to the management of the associated corporation's bank accounts and related documentation;
(b) providing advisory service to the associated corporation on its asset-liability management and formulation of dividend policy; and
(c) providing assistance to the associated corporation in relation to its acquisition of another associated corporation's business.

All the above services could be treated as corporate treasury services:
(i) Item (a) was related to the management of the cash and liquidity position of the associated corporation and therefore was covered by s.1(1)(a) of Schedule 17B.
(ii) Item (b) was a normal activity in capital budgeting falling within s.1(1)(d) of Schedule 17B.
(iii) The service in item (c) was related to the acquisition of a business by CTC-HK's associated corporation and was covered by s.1(1)(i) of Schedule 17B.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# Standalone entity
To qualify as a QCTC, the CTC cannot carry out other non-corporate treasury activity, subject to the safe harbour rule. Only activities that generate income to the CTC are considered for the purpose of determining whether the CTC has carried out any non-corporate treasury activity s.14D(4)). Therefore, a Hong Kong headquarter of an overseas corporation may qualify as a QCTC even though it performs corporate treasury activities as well as other corporate supporting functions for its group companies provided that those corporate supporting activities do not generate any income. Moreover, expense transactions (e.g. borrowings from FIs) would not preclude the CTC from being a QCTC. Therefore:

(a) A trading or manufacturing company with a corporate treasury division carrying out corporate treasury activities for group companies cannot qualify for profits tax concession, unless the [[safe harbor rule under s.14E]] is satisfied (DIPN 52, para 48).

(b) If a corporation takes a lease of office premises for carrying out corporate treasury transactions in relation to a non-Hong Kong associated corporation's business, the transaction of leasing premises would not preclude the corporation from being qualified as a QCTC because this is an expense transaction (DIPN 52, para 49).

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# safe harbor rule under s.14E
If a CTC undertakes other activities in Hong Kong, it may still be regarded as a QCTC if it satisfies the prescribed safe harbour rule. A CTC satisfies the sale harbor rule for a year of assessment if it falls within the 1-year safe harbor or the multiple-year safe harbour (s.14E(1)).

(a) **1-year safe harbour** – passes both the corporate treasury profits ('CTP') and corporate treasury assets ('CTA') tests for the year of assessment concerned (ss.14E(1)(a) & (2));

(b) **Multiple-year safe harbour** – the average percentages of the CTP and CTA for the year of assessment concerned and the preceding one\* or two years of assessment pass both tests (ss.14E(1)(b), (3) and (4)).

(\* if the CTC carries on a business in Hong Kong for less than 2 years)
---- 
The CTP test is satisfied if the CTP are not lower than 75% of the total profits, which is calculated based on the accounting profits irrespective of the source of profits. If there is substantial loss, the IRD would consider excluding the loss when computing the percentage for the sale harbour rule.

The CTA test is satisfied if the CTA are not lower than 75% of the total assets, which is calculated based on audited accounts irrespective of the location of the assets. The CTA include fixed assets that are used to carry out the corporate treasury activities, e.g. office equipment. The CTA are apportioned if they are partly used for carrying out a corporate treasury activity and partly for another purpose (s.14E(9)).

If a holding company also acts as a CTC, the Commissioner is prepared to exclude the equity investments in associated corporations and dividends from the denominators (i.e. total profits or assets) in calculating the CTP and CTA percentages.

![](image-195.png)
![](assets/image%202.png)

## Commissioner's determination
If neither of the above conditions are satisfied, the Commissioner may, on application by the taxpayer, exercise his discretion to determine that a CTC is a QCTC if he is of the opinion that the conditions specified in s.14D(3) or the safe harbour rule under s.14E would, in the ordinary course of business of the corporation, have been satisfied for the year of assessment (s.14F(3)).

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# s.16(2)(g) deduction rules for interest expenses incurred by intra-group financing businesses
A 'in-house' bank may be taxed on the interest income but not allowed a tax deduction for the interest expense due to the failure to satisfy any of the conditions in ss.16(2)(a) to (f). S.16(2)(g) is introduced with effect from 1 April 2016 to rectify the asymmetrical tax treatment of interest income and interest expense for genuine intra-group borrowing and lending transactions. The new deduction rules apply to the intra-group financing business carried on by a corporation, irrespective of whether the corporation is a QCTC (eligible for the concessionary tax rate), or carrying on other businesses in addition to an intra-group financing business. The new rules are discussed in details in section 8.5 on 'Deductible interest under ss.16(2)(g), 16(2CA) and 16(2CC)'.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# s.15(1)(ia) deeming provisions for interest income and other gains from intra-group financing businesses
The new legislation includes two deeming provisions to tax interest and other gains that arise through or from the carrying on of an intra-group financing business by a corporation in Hong Kong in the same way a FI would be taxed, effective from 3 June 2016.

Under s.15(1)(ia), interest income received by or accrued to a corporation (other than a FI) through or from the carrying on in Hong Kong of its intra-group financing business are **deemed taxable**, even if the moneys in respect of which the interest is received or accrues are ~made available outside Hong Kong~. In other words, the provision of credit test will no longer apply, and corporations which have applied this test to determine the source of interest will be affected.

The IRD reiterated in DIPN 52 that the operations test applies to determine the source of interest income for intra-group financing business, while the provision of credit test applies to determine the source of interest income for simple inter-company loans not made in the ordinary course of an intra-group financing business.
[[4.5 Reference to DIPNs]]
# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# invest in HK bonds (s.14D(8))
### excluded from qualifying profits - fund invest to bond issued in HK as issuer can claim tax deduction
Where any sum payable to the CTC in respect of any of the above [[corporate treasury activities]] can be claimed by any person as a ~tax deductible expense~ in Hong Kong, such sum will be excluded from the qualifying profits (s.14D(8)). Therefore, when a QCTC obtains funds from a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]] and ~invests the funds in bonds~ issued by a corporation ~carrying on business in Hong Kong~, the interest income would not qualify for the concessionary tax rate. This is because the **bond issuer would claim a tax deduction** in Hong Kong in respect of the interest payment.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# overseas bank deposit (s.15(1)(ia)
### deemed taxable (concessionary tax rate) - Invest the funds as overseas bank deposits - interest income
Where a QCTC obtains funds from a non-Hong Kong associated corporation and invests the funds as overseas bank deposits, the interest income is deemed taxable under s.15(1)(ia) (discussed in section 5.7.3 below) but would qualify for the concessionary tax rate. This is presumably because (i) the obtaining of funds by the QCTC from associated corporations is related to the business of the associated corporations; and (ii) the QCTC investing the same as overseas bank deposits is undertaken with a view to managing the cash and liquidity position of the QCTC or the associated corporations. As such, the placement of the overseas bank deposit is a corporate treasury transaction qualifying for the concessionary tax rate ~where no person will claim the interest paid to the QCTC as tax deductible in Hong Kong~.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# Qualifying profits at concessionary tax rate of 8.25%
The half rate concession only applies to **qualifying profits** (s.14D(1)), i.e. profits derived from the following qualifying transactions or services:
(a) Money lent to a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]] in the ordinary course of an [[intragroup financing business]].
(b) Qualifying [[corporate treasury services]] provided to a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]].
(c) Qualifying [[corporate treasury transactions]] entered into by a QCTC on its own account and related to the business of a [[non-Hong Kong associated corporation]].

1. [[invest in HK bonds (s.14D(8))]] - not qualify
2. [[overseas bank deposit (s.15(1)(ia)]] - deem

### non-qualifying profits not eligible for the concessionary tax rate
Even though a corporation satisfies the conditions of a QCTC, the following non-qualifying profits are not eligible for the concessionary tax rate (DIPN 52, para 82):
(a) Income from intra-group financing transaction under which money is lent to a Hong Kong associated corporation;
(b) Corporate treasury service income from a Hong Kong associated corporation;
(c) Income from corporate treasury transaction that is related to the business of a Hong Kong associated corporation;
(d) Income from corporate treasury transaction that is not related to the business of an associated corporation.

### apportion
Where the corporate treasury transaction relates to both the business of Hong Kong and **non-Hong Kong** associated corporations, profits will be ~apportioned~ and only profits related to the business of non-Hong Kong associated corporation can be taxed at the concessionary tax rate (DIPN 52, para 84).

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/CTC

# CTC example (2)
Example 31 (Adapted from DIPN 52, Example 19)

Corporation-HK is a trading company resident in Hong Kong. For the purpose of funding the acquisition of plant and machinery by Corporation-F, its associated corporation resident in Jurisdiction-F, Corporation-HK lent two loans totalling $20 million to Corporation-F at an interest rate of 1.5% per annum. The loans were made available to Corporation-F through CorporationHK's bank account in Jurisdiction-F.

As the two inter-company loan transactions ~did not constitute the carrying on of an intra-group financing business~, s.15(1)(ia) was not applicable. Applying the provision of credit test, the interest income received by Corporation-HK in respect of the two inter-company loans would not be chargeable to profits tax.

# QP/D/Tax/Profits/Deduction

# trade, profession or business
## 2.1 Trade
[[trade]] usually connotes some activities. Whether a trade is carried on is a question of fact to be determined by looking at all the circumstances of the case. Its existence is often determined by the **six badges of trade** (arrived at by the Royal Commission on the Taxation of Profits and Income in 1955) as follows:

[[1. Subject matter of the realisation]] 
[[2. Motive]]
[[3. Length of ownership]]
[[4. Frequency of similar transactions]]
[[5. Supplementary work done]]
[[6. Circumstances responsible for the realisation]]

The badges of trade are ~by no means exhaustive~. It is important to consider the **relevant facts and merits** of each case. Other relevant factors will also be considered:

(a) Method and reason of acquisition – If the asset is not acquired through purchase (e.g.

through inheritance), it is more likely that a trade is not carried on.

(b) Trading interest in the same field – If the person is engaged in the same field and shows expertise or specialised knowledge of the commodity, it is more likely that he is trading in the asset. For example, a property agent is more likely to be trading in properties.

(c) Method of financing the acquisition – If the asset is acquired with short-term finance such as bank overdraft, it is likely that the asset is acquired with the purpose of quick disposal for profit; particularly in property transactions.

(d) Utilisation of sale proceeds – The way the sale proceeds were put into use may indicate the purpose for sale and thus the intention of the person carrying on such a business. For example, the sale money may have been retained for use in a similar activity or for making another form of investment.

(e) Classification of asset in the accounts – If the asset is shown as a current asset or trading stock in the accounts of a business, it is very likely that the asset is acquired for trading purposes.

[[Profits tax - Example 1 - trade]]
[[Profits tax - Example 2 - trade]]
---- 
## 2.2 Profession
The term 'profession' is not defined in the IRO.

In IRC v Maxse [(1919) 1 KB 647], the COA stated as follows:

'a profession in the present use of language involves the idea of an occupation requiring either purely intellectual skill, or of any manual skill, as in painting and sculpture, or surgery, skill controlled by the intellectual skill of the operator, as distinguished from an occupation which is substantially the production, or sale, or arrangement for the production or sale of commodities.'

A profession usually involves the **exercise of intellectual skill** or manual skill controlled by intellectual knowledge. In practice, most professions also fall within the meaning of business.
---- 
## 2.3 Business
[[Business s.2]]
The tax position is as follows:
![](image-198.png)
The term 'business' is considered to have a wider meaning than that of trade. In practice, business implies activities of a commercial character. Whether a business is carried on in Hong Kong is a matter of fact. It will depend on the nature and extent of the activities of the person.
- [[Lee Yee Shing and Another v CIR (2008)]]

Where trade and profession are normally associated with some **active function**, the wider term business includes those circumstances where there is a **purely passive receipt** of income. Whether the passive receipt of interest by a company constitutes the carrying on of a business depends on the facts of each particular case. In [[DIPN 13]]

Back to back loan in [[CIR v Bartica Investment Ltd [(1966) 4 HKTC 129}]], 

mutual insurance companies, clubs and trade associations trade only with members

## Taxation of financial instruments and foreign exchange differences DIPN 42
# Taxation of financial instruments and foreign exchange differences: DIPN 42
## Financial instruments
In November 2005, the IRD issued DIPN 42 and mentioned that the decision by the CFA in Secan and Ranon has reaffirmed the general principle that, subject to statutory modifications, in the measurement of profits/losses or the [[timing of assessment DIPN 42]], the *ordinary principles of commercial accounting should be followed*. Thus, in deciding when and how the profit or loss derived from a financial instrument is to be recognised or measured, the **accounting treatments under [[HKAS 39 Financial Instruments]] are relevant,** except
	- where there is a specific express statutory provision ::or:: 
	- where the accounting classification and the legal classification of a financial instrument differ. 
[[Financial Instruments]]

It should be pointed out that the **accounting treatments**, by itself, cannot operate to change the character of an asset from investment to trading and vice versa. Whether the asset is of [[Capital vs Revenue nature]] is a question of ~fact and degree and all the surrounding circumstances~, including the accounting treatment, have to be considered. Well established tax principles like the '[[badges of trade]]’ will continue to be applicable. In deciding whether a financial instrument is a capital or trading asset, the **intention** ~at the time of acquisition~ of the financial instrument is always relevant.

[[Profits tax - Example 17 unrealized gain]]
[[Profits tax - example 18 convertible bonds]]
---- 
## Derivatives
+ [[Derivative]] - A financial asset or financial liability at fair value through profit or loss includes a financial asset or financial liability that is held for trading. Unless a derivative is a ~designated and effective~ [[hedging instrument]], it will be **classified as held for trading**. The **change** in fair value and gain or loss on disposal will be ~taxable or deductible~, as the case may be.
+ Insurance of finance business - Financial instruments held by a **FI** or a taxpayer which carries on an insurance, a money lending, securities dealing or finance business should be regarded as **trading assets** as they are often acquired in the course of the business ~with a view to resale at a profit~ (see Sincere Insurance and Investment Co Ltd (1 HKTC 602)).
+ Currency [[forward contracts]] - 
	+ The gain or loss arising from currency forward contract acquired for the purpose of ~hedging the future payment of a capital asset~ like machinery is **capital** in nature. It will be taken into account in computing ~[[Depreciation allowances]]~ for the capital asset. 
	+ If the currency forward contract is acquired for the purpose of ~hedging the purchase of trading stock~, the relevant gain or loss is **revenue** in nature. By the same token, the profit or loss on an interest rate contract [[interest rate futures]] acquired to protect future increase in interest cost of borrowing used to finance the purchase of trading stock is **revenue** in nature.
- [[HKFRS 9: Hedging]] hedge accounting: if the hedging relationship **qualifies** for hedge accounting under HKAS 39 and is accounted for as such, the IRD considers that the [[hedged item]] and the [[hedging instrument]] ~should not be considered separately~ because hedging is an attempt to mitigate the impact of economic risks of the hedged items. The [[Locality]] of the [[hedging instrument]] should **follow** that of the [[hedged item]]. 
	- If the hedged item and the hedging instrument ~are accounted for separately~ in the accounts, the **facts and circumstances** of each individual case need to be examined to determine whether the hedging instrument is really a hedge against the hedged item. 
	- If the hedging instrument is as ~a matter of fact a hedge against the hedged item~, the hedged item and the hedging instrument ~may not be considered separately~. 
	- Regarding the nature of the profit or loss, capital or revenue arising from the hedging instrument, the IRD accepts that it **depends on the nature of the hedged item**.
- [[HKFRS 9: embedded derivatives]] - The IRD considers that the nature (capital or revenue) and locality of profit arising from an embedded derivative (e.g. put options on bonds, callable bonds, put options on preference shares) and its host contract should be determined on the basis that it is **one single instrument**, and the ~same tax treatment~ will be applied.
---- 
## Exchange differences
- [[exchange differences]] - HKAS 21 deals with the effects of changes in foreign exchange rates. Under DIPN 42, all taxpayers including FIs should treat 
	- exchange gains or losses of a trading nature and recognised in the income statement, whether realised or not, as taxable receipts or deductible expenses. An adjustment in the tax computation on the ground that an exchange difference has not yet realised are no longer accepted by the IRD. 
	- Nevertheless, the exchange gains or losses of a capital nature or arising in or derived from outside Hong Kong are still neither taxable nor allowable.

The CFI considered, in Nice Cheer, that unlike trading securities, unrealised gains are not taxable and should not apply to foreign exchange transactions. Unrealised gains in foreign exchange transactions are different from those in trading securities transactions because the underlying trading assets in foreign exchange transactions are foreign currencies, i.e. fungible assets that have **a ready market and a value** against the reporting currency. These gains are not 'anticipated' but ~actual accrued profits valued~ on the year end date. Therefore, unrealised exchange gains recorded at the year end date are treated as profits and are **taxable**.

[[Profits tax - Example 19 - exchange gain]]

# qualifying aircraft leasing management activity
An aircraft leasing management activity carried out by a corporation in respect of an aircraft is a 'qualifying aircraft leasing management activity' if (s.14G(7)):
(a) The activity is carried out in the ordinary course of the QALM's business carried on in Hong Kong;
(b) The activity is carried out for a QAL in respect of an aircraft owned by the QAL, and is leased to an aircraft operator, when the activity is carried out.

When, at the request of a relevant QAL, a QALM provides finance to an airline enterprise for acquiring an aircraft from the relevant QAL, the QALM is assisting the QAL to dispose of an aircraft. Such activity is regarded as having been carried out for the relevant QAL and would qualify for the profits tax concession if other criteria are satisfied (DIPN 54, para. 45).

## FE (Jun 18) Paper II Q5(a) stamp duty
# FE (Jun 18) Paper II: Q5(a) stamp duty
(a) Upon the disposal of the shares of WT Tours, advise (i) the amount of stamp duty payable; (ii) the timing of stamping if the transfer takes place outside of Hong Kong; (iii) the penalty for late stamping if it is late by 1.5 months; and (iv) the penalty for late stamping if it is late by one year.

(4 marks)
---- 
[[FE (Jun 18) Paper II: case]]
## Solutions
(i) 0.2% of the higher of the consideration or market value of the shares is payable on the bought note (0.1%) and sold note (0.1%).

In addition, HK$5 is payable on the instrument of transfer.

(ii) For the transfer of shares outside Hong Kong, stamping should be made within 30 days from the date of transfer.

(iii) Four times the stamp duty is payable as the penalty for late stamping exceeding one month but not more than two months.

(iv) Ten times the stamp duty is payable as the penalty for late stamping ~exceeding two months~.

# QP/Practice/Tax/Stamp

# stamp duty Example 1
A owes B $5 million and is in financial difficulties. The parties agree that A will assign to B his immovable property with a value of $4.5 million as full settlement of the debt.

Stamp duty payable on the conveyance will be based on $5 million. However, the duty-payer may apply to the Collector to have the stamp duty payable based on the value of the property of $4.5 million.

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# stamp duty Example 2
E sells the shares in C Ltd to D. C Ltd owns a property with a market value of $5 million and an outstanding mortgage of $2 million. D agrees to acquire the shares in C Ltd by paying E $3 million and undertaking repayment of the $2 million liability.

Stamp duty payable on the conveyance will be based on $5 million, being cash paid plus value of the debt assigned.

# RPPT
'Residential property' means immovable property other than [[non-RPPT]].

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# non-RPPT
'Non-residential property' means immovable property which may not be used at any time for residential purposes under the existing conditions of:
- (a) a Government lease or an agreement for a Government lease;
- (b) a deed of mutual covenant, within the meaning of s.2 of the Building Management Ordinance;
- (c) an occupation permit issued under s.21 of the Buildings Ordinance; or
- (d) any other instrument which, the Collector is satisfied, effectively restricts the permitted use of the property.

The classification of the property is by reference to the permitted use rather than the actual use.

# (B) When AVD is exempt for:
(a) Nomination of a close relative(s) (be they HKPRs or not) who do(es) not own any other RPPT in Hong Kong at the time of nomination.

(b) Transfer of a property to a beneficiary of the estate of a deceased person in accordance with that provided under a will or the law of intestacy; or acquired the property by the right of survivorship.

(c) Acquisition or transfer of a property by or to a body corporate from an associated body corporate.

(d) Acquisition or transfer of properties by or to the Government.

(e) Gift of properties received by charitable institutions exempted from tax under s.88 of the IRO.

# **Stamp Duty**

image.png
** Overview of stamp duty**

Stamp duty is a tax on instruments or documents levied under the Stamp Duty Ordinance (Chapter 117) ('SDO'). The SDO is made up of **seven parts** with ss.1 to 71 and nine schedules. In this chapter, all references to statutory provisions are references to the SDO unless otherwise stated. The **SDO** is administered by the Stamp Office which is a part of the IRD, and the officer in charge is the Collector of Stamp Revenue ('the Collector') who is also the Commissioner. With the growth of **e-commerce**, the Government has also introduced an alternative way of stamping certain instruments in the form of an electronic record.

[instrument s.2](bear://x-callback-url/open-note?title=instrument%20s%2E2&x-error=bear%3A%2F%2Fx%2Dcallback%2Durl%2Fcreate%3Ftitle%3Dinstrument%2520s%252E2) An 'instrument' is defined in s.2 as including 'every written document'. Provided that an instrument falls within one of the following Heads of charge, it will be **stampable** whether or not that instrument was executed in or outside Hong Kong:

[Head 1 Immovable property in Hong Kong](bear://x-callback-url/open-note?title=Head%201%20Immovable%20property%20in%20Hong%20Kong&x-error=bear%3A%2F%2Fx%2Dcallback%2Durl%2Fcreate%3Ftitle%3DHead%25201%2520Immovable%2520property%2520in%2520Hong%2520Kong)
- [lease stamp duty (Head 1(2))](bear://x-callback-url/open-note?title=lease%20stamp%20duty%20%28Head%201%282%29%29&x-error=bear%3A%2F%2Fx%2Dcallback%2Durl%2Fcreate%3Ftitle%3Dlease%2520stamp%2520duty%2520%2528Head%25201%25282%2529%2529)
Head 2 Hong Kong stock
Head 3 Hong Kong bearer instrument
Head 4 Duplicates and counterparts of chargeable instruments under Heads 1, 2 and 3

1. Theoretically, stamp duty is **levied on instruments or documents**, not on transactions. 
2. If a transaction can be effected verbally or by conduct, no stamp duty is chargeable. 
- However, for some of the transactions which are not effected by an instrument or a document, there are **provisions under the SDO or other Ordinances requiring a document to be made for stamping**. For example,
	- (a) all conveyances of land or buildings must be by way of deed;
	- (b) an agreement for sale and purchase ('AFS') of immovable property must be evidenced in writing;
	- (c) a lease of immovable property for a period exceeding three years must be in writing;
	- (d) in the case of sale and purchase of Hong Kong stock, the buyer and the seller or their brokers are required under s.19 to execute contract notes (sold note for the seller, bought note for the buyer) for stamping.
		- S.19 also **deems** a **verbal agreement** to transfer the beneficial interest in Hong Kong stock, other than by sale and purchase, to be a sale and purchase of Hong Kong stock and the parties to the transaction are required to execute contract notes, which are chargeable to stamp duty. Even if the required document is not made, liability to stamp duty is still recoverable by the Collector.

Stamp duty may either be fixed (e.g. $5 for a duplicate under Head 4) or ad valorem (e.g. 0.2% on contract notes, based on the value of stock transferred under Head 2).

The Stamp Office is not responsible for ascertaining the legality of any document or instrument before stamping. An illegal document (e.g. a lease agreement for subletting a flat owned by the Housing Authority) may still be stamped. On the other hand, instruments not properly stamped will not be acted upon, filed or registered by any public officer or body corporate.

[To deter speculations in the residential property ('RPPT') market](bear://x-callback-url/open-note?title=To%20deter%20speculations%20in%20the%20residential%20property%20%28%27RPPT%27%29%20market&x-error=bear%3A%2F%2Fx%2Dcallback%2Durl%2Fcreate%3Ftitle%3DTo%2520deter%2520speculations%2520in%2520the%2520residential%2520property%2520%2528%2527RPPT%2527%2529%2520market), the government has launched a series of tax measures including the following:

## Overview of stamp duty
Stamp duty is a ~tax on instruments or documents~ levied under the Stamp Duty Ordinance (Chapter 117) ('SDO'). The SDO is made up of **seven parts** with ss.1 to 71 and nine schedules. In this chapter, all references to statutory provisions are references to the SDO unless otherwise stated. The **SDO** is administered by the ~Stamp Office~ which is a part of the IRD, and the officer in charge is the Collector of Stamp Revenue ('the Collector') who is also the Commissioner. With the growth of **e-commerce**, the Government has also introduced an alternative way of stamping certain ~instruments in the form of an electronic record~.

[[instrument s.2]] An 'instrument' is defined in s.2 as including 'every written document'. Provided that an instrument falls within one of the following Heads of charge, it will be **stampable** whether or not that instrument was executed in or outside Hong Kong:

[[Head 1 Immovable property in Hong Kong]]
	- [[lease stamp duty (Head 1(2))]]
Head 2 Hong Kong stock
Head 3 Hong Kong bearer instrument
Head 4 Duplicates and counterparts of chargeable instruments under Heads 1, 2 and 3

1. Theoretically, stamp duty is **levied on instruments or documents**, not on transactions. 
2. If a transaction can be effected verbally or by conduct, no stamp duty is chargeable. 
	- However, for some of the transactions which are not effected by an instrument or a document, there are **~provisions under the SDO or other Ordinances requiring a document to be made for stamping~**. For example,
		- (a) all conveyances of land or buildings must be by way of deed;
		- (b) an agreement for sale and purchase ('AFS') of immovable property must be evidenced in writing;
		- (c) a lease of immovable property for a period exceeding three years must be in writing;
		- (d) in the case of sale and purchase of Hong Kong stock, the buyer and the seller or their brokers are required under s.19 to execute contract notes (sold note for the seller, bought note for the buyer) for stamping.
			- S.19 also **deems** a **verbal agreement** to ~transfer the beneficial interest in Hong Kong stock~, other than by sale and purchase, to be a ~sale and purchase of Hong Kong stock~ and the parties to the transaction are required to execute contract notes, which are chargeable to stamp duty. Even if the required document is not made, liability to stamp duty is still recoverable by the Collector.

Stamp duty may either be fixed (e.g. $5 for a duplicate under Head 4) or ad valorem (e.g. 0.2% on contract notes, based on the value of stock transferred under Head 2).

The ~Stamp Office~ is not responsible for ascertaining the legality of any document or instrument before stamping. An illegal document (e.g. a lease agreement for subletting a flat owned by the Housing Authority) may still be stamped. On the other hand, instruments not properly stamped will not be acted upon, filed or registered by any public officer or body corporate.

(a) Increase in stamp duty rate on property transactions On 22 February 2013, the Financial Secretary announced that the Government would amend the Stamp Duty Ordinance to adjust the ad valorem stamp duty (AVD) rates. Unless specifically exempted or otherwise provided, the new AVD rates for both residential and nonresidential properties are as follows.

![](image-200.png)

Refer to chapter 8 for details.

(b) Introduction of Special Stamp Duty The Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2011 was enacted on 30 June 2011 to introduce a special stamp duty (SSD) which would be imposed on disposal of residential properties which were acquired by the vendor on or after 20 November 2010 and resold within 24 months from the date of acquisition. The SSD would be imposed on top of the normal stamp duty currently payable on conveyance on sale of immovable properties, with a few exemptions available.

In December 2012, the government introduced a Bill increasing each of the existing three levels of SDD rates by 5%. In addition, it extends the coverage period from 24 months to 36 months. The enhanced special stamp duty rates were passed by Legislative Council on 22 February 2014 and would have retrospective effect from 27 October 2012.

The seller and the buyer are jointly and severally liable for paying the SSD which is calculated based on the stated consideration or market value, whichever is higher, of the resold property at the following regressive rates, with the higher rate for shorter holding periods:
Refer to chapter 8 for details.

(b) Introduction of Special Stamp Duty The Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2011 was enacted on 30 June 2011 to introduce a special stamp duty (SSD) which would be imposed on disposal of residential properties which were acquired by the vendor on or after 20 November 2010 and resold within 24 months from the date of acquisition. The SSD would be imposed on top of the normal stamp duty currently payable on conveyance on sale of immovable properties, with a few exemptions available.

In December 2012, the government introduced a Bill increasing each of the existing three levels of SDD rates by 5%. In addition, it extends the coverage period from 24 months to 36 months. The enhanced special stamp duty rates were passed by Legislative Council on 22 February 2014 and would have retrospective effect from 27 October 2012.

The seller and the buyer are jointly and severally liable for paying the SSD which is calculated based on the stated consideration or market value, whichever is higher, of the resold property at the following regressive rates, with the higher rate for shorter holding periods:
Refer to chapter 8 for details.

(c) Buyer's stamp duty on acquisition of residential properties

Buyer's stamp duty (BSD) on acquisition of Hong Kong residential properties by any person (including Hong Kong and foreign companies) other than a Hong Kong permanent resident would be charged at a flat rate of 15% of the stated consideration or the market value of the property acquired, whichever is higher.

The BSD would be imposed on top of the ad valorem stamp duty and the SSD, if applicable.

The BSD was passed by Legislative Council on 22 February 2014 and would have retrospective effect from 27 October 2012.

(d) Waiver of stamp duty for transfer of shares or units of Exchange Traded Funds

The Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2015 was gazetted on 13 February 2015 to implement the stamp duty waiver for the transfer of shares or units of all exchange traded funds (ETFs). The stamp duty waiver will be conducive to fostering Hong Kong's position as an asset management centre and the development of our financial services sector.

(e) 15% AVD on residential properties

The Stamp Duty (Amendment) Bill 2017 (the Bill) was gazetted on 27 January 2017.

The Bill aims to implement the new demand-side management measure approved by the Chief Executive-in-Council and announced on November 4, 2016, i.e. to introduce a new flat rate of 15% for AVD chargeable on residential property transactions, in lieu of the existing AVD rates at Scale 1. The new measure took effect from November 5, 2016.

The Government announced the tightening up of exemption arrangement for Hong Kong permanent residents under the measure of 15% AVD on residential properties on 11 April 2017 (i.e. if a Hong Kong permanent resident acquires more than one residential property under a single instrument, the transaction concerned will no longer be exempted). The tightened up exemption arrangement took effect from 12 April 2017.

Refer to chapter 8 for details.

## FE (Jun 18) Paper II Q5(b) intra-group stamp duty
# FE (Jun 18) Paper II: Q5(b) intra-group stamp duty
(b) Analyse if intra-group relief for stamp duty is possible. If not, state the reason and advise whether there is another way to mitigate the stamp duty payable. Advise as to how it could be carried out, if applicable, and state any assumption(s).

(7 marks)
[[FE (Jun 18) Paper II: case]]
---- 
## Solutions
`Stamp duty relief under s.45` is not applicable because (i) there is a plan that Newco Ltd (as transferee) would ~leave the group~; or (ii) Newco Ltd (as transferee) would ~leave the group two months~ after the transfer, which does not exceed the required **two years’ period** under s.45.

It is possible for WT Tours to **distribute a portion of the retained profits** of HK$19 million in the form of a **dividend**, provided such portion is distributable, before the transfer of shares of WT Tours. After the distribution, the consideration or the market value of the shares of WT Tours would be lower, hence this could mitigate the stamp duty payable.

This may also save the efforts of the buyer of Newco Ltd in ascertaining how much retained profits of WT Tours are distributable or not, thus simplifying the [[due diligence]] process. This ~reason should be documented~ in order to avoid any general avoidance challenge (Ramsay step plan challenge under Arrowtown case).

# QP/Practice/Tax/Stamp

# To deter speculations in the residential property ('RPPT') market
- The maximum rate of ad valorem duty ('AVD') for property transactions valued more than $20 million was increased to 4.25%, effective from 1 April 2010.
- A special stamp duty ('SSD') was enacted on 30 June 2011 (see section 3.3 on 'Special stamp duty').
- Two further measures, comprising a measure to enhance the SSD rates and the introduction of a 15% buyer's stamp duty ('BSD'), were enacted on 22 February 2014 (see section 3.4 on 'Buyer's stamp duty').
- To discourage speculations in the property market (both residential and non-residential), the maximum AVD rate was further increased from 4.25% to 8.5%, effective from 23 February 2013.
- Finally, on 4 November 2016, the Government announced that the SDO would be amended to increase the AVD rates for RPPT transactions to a flat rate of 15% (see section 3.1.1 on 'Rates of ad valorem duty').

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# Scope of charge - Stamp duty
Stamp duty is charged on instruments specified in the First Schedule under the four Heads of charges:

[[Head 1 Immovable property in Hong Kong]]
Head 2 Hong Kong stock
Head 3 Hong Kong bearer instrument
Head 4 Duplicates and counterparts of chargeable instruments under Heads 1, 2 and 3

An instrument must be stamped for its leading and principal object. If a chargeable instrument contains separate and distinct matters, such matters will be separately stamped as if they were separate instruments under more than one Head.

The place of execution of the instruments does not affect the chargeability to stamp duty. It only affects the time of stamping (s.10(2)).

[[chargeable instruments]]

## Substance over form
When considering whether an instrument is chargeable with stamp duty, the principle of 'substance over form' is applied. The Collector will look at the substance, the nature of the agreement; rather than the form of, the name of, or the label put on the instrument.

For example, both a lease and a license give the tenant and licensee a right to occupy an immovable property. However, a lease agreement provides the tenant with an exclusive right of possession while a license agreement provides the licensee a right of occupation which may be revoked by the licensor at will (e.g. the right of a hotel guest). As a lease is a stampable instrument under Head 1(2) but a licence agreement is not, a duty-payer may label an agreement which grants an exclusive right of possession as a license for the purpose of avoiding stamp duty. In such circumstances, the Collector will ignore the label and stamp the agreement as a lease.

[[Stampable consideration]]

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# Stampable consideration
Stamp duty is levied on the **value of consideration** which may be made up of money, money's worth, debts assigned or waived, securities, commodities or services performed. If the stated consideration is ~less than the market value~ of the immovable property or stock transferred, stamp duty is chargeable on the **market value**. Hence, the stampable value of:
	- (a) **immovable property** is based on the **market value** of the property free from ~any encumbrance~; and
	- (b) **stock** is based on the **net asset value** of the stock determined with reference to the latest accounts of the company and market value of the assets at the time of transfer.

If there is no stated consideration, the instrument is regarded as a ~voluntary disposition inter vivos~ (i.e. a gift made during lifetime), and stamp duty is chargeable on the **market value** of the immovable property or stock transferred (see section 7 on 'Voluntary disposition inter vivos').

## Consideration consisting of stock
Pursuant to s.22(1), where the consideration or any part of the consideration for a COS consists of any stock, stamp duty is chargeable by reference to the **value of the stock** ~on the date of conveyance or transfer~.

## Consideration consisting of security not being stock
Pursuant to s.22(2), where the consideration or any part of the consideration for a COS consists of any security which is not stock, stamp duty is chargeable by reference to ~the amount due on the date of conveyance or transfer~ for the **principal and interest** upon the security.

## Consideration consisting of debts payable by the transferee
SS.24(1) provides that debts, including contingent ones, payable by the transferee are treated as **part of the consideration** for a conveyance of immovable property or transfer of stock that is chargeable to stamp duty.

## Consideration in the form of debts waived
Under s.24(1), debts waived by the transferee are treated as **part of the consideration** for a conveyance of immovable property or transfer of stock. If the debt consideration exceeds the value of the property conveyed or stock transferred, stamp duty is chargeable based on the higher amount of the debt to be settled by the immovable property or stock. However, pursuant to s.24(2), the person liable for the stamp duty may apply to have the stamp duty payable based on the ~lower value of the immovable property or stock~. In such case, the chargeable instrument (the conveyance or contract notes) has to be adjudicated (see section 9.5 on 'Adjudication').

[[stamp duty Example 1]]

## Consideration in the form of debts assigned
Pursuant to s.24(3), when there is a **transfer of a beneficial interest** in a body corporate and the transferee will incur liability in respect of any **indebtedness** of the body corporate, the amount of the indebtedness will form part of the consideration for the transfer.

[[stamp duty Example 2]]

SOIPN 3 (para 21) provides guidance on deemed consideration under s.24 and examples as to the practical application of s.24.

## Consideration consisting of periodic payments
If consideration consists of periodic payments, stamp duty is charged under s.23 as follows:
![](67D3AC2C-0497-4A07-9FB2-6AF8793152FB.png)

## Consideration expressed in foreign currency
For the purpose of calculating the stampable value, the consideration is translated into Hong Kong dollars at the rate of exchange prevailing on the date of the instrument. As defined in s.18(2), the 'rate of exchange' means the buying rate for the currency in question, as determined by the Monetary Authority, for telegraphic transfers at the commencement of business on the date of the instrument or, if that date is a Sunday or a general holiday, on the business day immediately preceding that date.

## Contingency principle
Stamp duty is assessed on the basis of the circumstances prevailing at the time an instrument is executed. Liability to stamp duty cannot be altered or affected by events subsequent to the execution. This so-called 'contingency principle' applies as follows:
(a) If the consideration under an instrument is unascertainable at the time of execution, no stamp duty can be assessed.
(b) If the consideration is uncertain but the instrument contains a clause on the amounts of maximum and minimum consideration payable, stamp duty is assessed on the maximum amount payable. Any duty paid will not be refunded even though the consideration payable at a later date is less than the maximum amount stated.
(c) If the consideration is uncertain but the instrument contains a clause on the amount of minimum consideration payable, stamp duty is assessed on the minimum amount payable. Further duty cannot be assessed even though the consideration payable at a later date is more than the minimum amount stated.

[[stamp duty Example 3]]

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# stamp duty Example 3
F leased a shop to a boutique owner under a lease for a term of three years, for a monthly rental of $10,000 plus 10% of the monthly turnover of the boutique.

(a) If there is no agreed maximum or minimum rental, stamp duty is assessed on the amount that is ascertainable at the time of execution, i.e. monthly rental of $10,000. Stamp duty payable is therefore 0.5% of average yearly rent, i.e. $600 ($10,000 x 12 x 0.5%) (see section 3.5.2 on 'Lease with premium and/or rent').

(b) If there are agreed maximum monthly rental of $60,000 and minimum monthly rental of $30,000, stamp duty is assessed on the maximum amount payable, i.e. monthly rental of $60,000. Stamp duty payable is therefore 0.5% of average yearly rent, i.e. $3,600 ($60,000 x 12 x 0.5%).

(c) If there is no maximum monthly rental but a minimum monthly rental of $30,000, stamp duty is assessed on the minimum amount payable, i.e. monthly rental of $30,000. Stamp duty payable is therefore 0.5% of average yearly rent, i.e. $1,800 ($30,000 x 12 x 0.5%).

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# Head 1 Immovable property in Hong Kong
The stamping of immovable property is governed by Head 1 in the First Schedule:

Head 1 Immovable property in Hong Kong
Head 1(1) COS chargeable with AVD
Head 1(1AA) COS chargeable with SSD
Head 1(1AAB) COS chargeable with BSD
Head 1(1A) AFS chargeable with AVD
Head 1(1B) AFS chargeable with SSD
Head 1(1C) AFS chargeable with BSD
Head 1(2) Lease

In accordance with s.3 of the Interpretation and General Clauses Ordinance, 'immovable property' means:
(a) land, whether covered by water or not;
(b) any estate, right, interest or easement in or over land; and
(c) things attached to land or permanently fastened to anything attached to land.

The definition includes both tangible land and buildings, and intangible rights in or over any land and buildings.

There are normally three instruments involved in the sale of immovable property, namely a provisional (temporary) AFS ('PAFS'), a formal AFS and a COS. Typically, the PAFS (or the formal AFS if it is executed within 14 days of signing the PAFS) of an immovable property is subject to AVD while the COS (if it is executed in conformity with the duly stamped AFS) is subject to a fixed duty of $100.

---- 
[[Conveyance on sale (Head 1(1))]]
# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# Conveyance on sale (Head 1(1))
s.2(1) '**Conveyance**' means 'every instrument (including a surrender) and every decree or order of any court whereby any immovable property is transferred to or vested in any person'.

'**Conveyance on sale**' means 'every conveyance whereby any immovable property, upon the sale thereof, is transferred to or vested in a purchaser or any other person on his behalf or by his direction, and includes a foreclosure order'.

This definition is considered to be wide enough to cover release and renunciations relating to immovable property. However, not every conveyance is a COS, e.g. a mortgage document or other legal charge over immovable property; and no stamp duty is payable if it is not.
---- 
## Chargeable under Head 1(1)
(a) **Deed of assignment** for the sale and purchase of an immovable property.

(b) **Deed of gift** of an immovable property or conveyance operating as a voluntary disposition inter vivos. Stamp duty is chargeable on the market value of the property (s.27(1)) (see Example 4 below).

(c) **Foreclosure order** relating to an immovable property whereby the mortgaged property is conveyed to the mortgagee (the lender which is usually the bank) as the mortgagor (the borrower) is unable to repay the debt. Foreclosure is the process by which the right of a mortgagor to redeem the mortgaged property is terminated, and the mortgagee becomes the owner of the mortgaged property at law and at equity. A foreclosure order must be granted by court decree.

(d) **Deed of exchange** for the exchange of an immovable property. By virtue of ss.25(7) and 27, stamp duty is chargeable on any consideration paid or given for equality (i.e. equality money paid by one owner to the other owner) or the difference between the values of the exchanged properties, whichever is the higher.

(e) **Deed of partition** in relation to an immovable property. By virtue of ss.25(7) and 27, stamp duty is chargeable on any consideration paid or given for equality or the difference between the values of the partitioned properties, whichever is the higher.

(f) **Deed of family arrangement** whereby a beneficiary takes an immovable property in satisfaction of his pecuniary legacy (see Example 5 below).
---- 
## rates of Ad Valorem Duty (AVD)
Before 4 November 2016, there are two scales of Ad Valorem Duty (AVD) rates for COS of immovable property as follows:

(a) Scale 2 rates apply to:
	- (i) properties acquired during 1 April 2010 to 22 February 2013; or
	- (ii) RPPTs acquired on or after 23 February 2013, where the purchaser/transferee is a Hong Kong permanent resident (‘[[HKPR]]’) who acquires the [[RPPT]] on his/her own behalf (i.e. the person is both the legal and beneficial owner) and owns no other RPPT in Hong Kong at the time of acquisition.
![](Study/QP/old%20LP/Doc/0927B4E0-49D3-47EF-9C5E-C737271282BE.png)

(b) Scale 1 rates apply to:
	- (i) any RPPTs acquired during the period from 23 February 2013 to 4 November 2016, except that acquired by a HKPR on his/her own behalf (i.e. the person is both the legal and beneficial owner) and who does not own any other RPPT in Hong Kong at the time of acquisition; and
	- (ii) all non-RPPTs acquired by either an individual or a company on or after 23 February 2013.
![](Study/QP/old%20LP/Doc/3C132600-D806-43CD-AC52-910E757CFDB7.png)
As an anti-avoidance measure, if a duty-payer wishes to enjoy the progressive rates rather than the maximum rate of 4.25% or 8.5%, he or she must include in the COS a s.29 certificate stating that the transaction does not form part of a larger transaction or a series of transactions, in respect of which the aggregate consideration or value exceeds the amount for that progressive rate.

In addition to the above AVD, the COS of RPPT may be subject to SSD (see section 3.3 on 'Special stamp duty') and BSD (see section 3.4 on 'Buyer's stamp duty') if no AFS was entered into.
---- 
### Scale 1 rates will not be applicable under the following circumstances
[[(A) When Scale 2 rates are applicable to:]]
[[(B) When AVD is exempt for:]]
(C) When entitled to a partial refund of AVD for:
	- Acquisition of a RPPT or non-RPPT (including bare sites) for the purpose of redevelopment.

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# HKPR
'HKPR' means a person who holds a valid Hong Kong permanent identity card ('PIC'), or who is eligible to but exempted from applying for the issue of a PIC (the aged, the blind or the infirm).

A person 'owns' a RPPT if he is the beneficial owner of such property, or any share or interest thereof.

# QP/D/Tax/Stamp

# (A) When Scale 2 rates are applicable to:
(a) Acquisition of a RPPT (whether or not together with a car parking space) by a HKPR who is acting on his/her own behalf, and does not own any other RPPT (and car parking space, if applicable) in Hong Kong at the time of acquisition.

(b) Acquisition of a RPPT (whether or not together with a car parking space) by two or more HKPRs jointly as co-owners or joint owners, and each of the purchasers is acting on his/her own behalf and does not own any other RPPT (and car parking space, if applicable) in Hong Kong at the time of acquisition.

(c) Acquisition of a RPPT by a HKPR jointly as a co-owner or joint owner with a close relative(s) who is/are not HKPR, and each of the purchasers is acting on his/her own behalf and does not own any other RPPT in Hong Kong at the time of acquisition. Close relatives include parent (but not parent-in-law), spouse, child, brother or sister who are blood-related, half-blood related, adopted or step-related. If there are more than two purchasers/transferees, all of them must be closely related.

(d) Acquisition or transfer of RPPT between close relatives, irrespective of whether they are HKPRs, and whether they are beneficial owners of any other RPPT in Hong Kong at the time of acquisition or transfer.

If there are more than two purchasers/transferees, all of them must be closely related.

(e) Nomination of a close relative(s) (be they HKPRs or not) who is/are owner(s) of other RPPT in Hong Kong at the time of nomination, to take up the assignment of a RPPT, and the nominee is acting on his/her own behalf. If there is more than one nominee, all the nominees must be close relatives. If the close relative is not a beneficial owner of any other RPPT in Hong Kong, the nomination is not an AFS and not chargeable with AVD.

(f) Acquisition or transfer of a property by a court order or pursuant to a court order, which includes a foreclosure order obtained by a mortgagee whether or not it falls under the definition of a FI within the meaning of s.2 of the IRO.

(g) Transfer/vesting of a mortgaged property under a conveyance to/in its mortgagee that is a FI within the meaning of s.2 of the IRO, or a receiver appointed by the mortgagee.

(h) Acquisition of a property by a person acting on his/her own behalf to replace another property which was owned by that person, and that has been:
	- (i) purchased or acquired pursuant to redevelopment projects pursued by the Urban Renewal Authority; or
	- (ii) resumed under an order made under s.3 or purchased under s.4A of the Lands Resumption Ordinance; or
	- (iii) sold pursuant to an order for sale made by the Lands Tribunal under s.4(1)(b)(i) of the Land (Compulsory Sale for Redevelopment) Ordinance; or
	- (iv) resumed under an order made under s.4(1) of the Mass Transit Railway (Land Resumption and Related Provisions) Ordinance; or
	- (v) resumed under an order made under s.13(1) of the Roads (Works, Use and Compensation) Ordinance; or
	- (vi) resumed under an order made under ss.16 or 28(1) of the Railway Ordinance; or
	- (vii) acquired under an acquisition order made under ss.3(1) or (2) of the Land Acquisition (Possessory Title) Ordinance; or
	- (viii) resumed under an order made under s.37(2) of the Land Drainage Ordinance.
